rows: CDM 2015 applies health-and-safety duties across construction projects from concept through completion.
Clients must make suitable arrangements so construction work can be managed safely and with adequate time and resources.
Projects should use people and organisations with suitable skills, knowledge, training and experience for their roles.
Dutyholders must cooperate and coordinate their work with others involved in the project.
Clients must provide relevant pre-construction information about the project and site.
A construction phase plan must be prepared before the construction phase begins.
For projects involving more than one contractor, a principal designer coordinates health and safety during pre-construction.
For projects involving more than one contractor, a principal contractor coordinates health and safety during construction.
Domestic-client duties can pass to other CDM dutyholders, so the named legal dutyholder must be confirmed.
Planning or property records do not prove that competence, coordination, information exchange or the construction phase plan are adequate.
Work must be planned and controlled to prevent danger to workers in or near excavations.
A competent person must inspect excavation supports or battering at the start of the working shift and at other specified times.
Work should not proceed until the excavation and its precautions are safe.
Pre-construction information should include ground conditions, underground structures, watercourses and existing services.
Excavation planning must address collapse, falling material, falls, nearby structures, services and water ingress.
Safe access and exit must be provided where people need to enter an excavation.
Temporary supports must be designed, installed, maintained and used for foreseeable loads and their intended purpose.
Excavation support and other temporary works require competent inspection and active management.
Ground strength, groundwater, weather and nearby loads are site-specific and can change after work begins.
A map or parcel record cannot verify support design, inspection status, service location or current excavation stability.
Demolition, dismantling and structural alteration must be planned and managed before work starts.
Arrangements for demolition, dismantling or structural alteration must be recorded in writing before the work begins.
Structural stability must be considered throughout the selected demolition sequence.
Clients and designers should provide available structural, service and hazardous-material information to those planning the work.
Utilities and stored energy must be identified and isolated or otherwise controlled before affected work proceeds.
Exclusion zones and controlled access are required where falling material or structural collapse could endanger people.
Demolition methods should account for asbestos, dust, noise, vibration, fire and adjacent structures.
Competent supervision must ensure the planned sequence and precautions are followed as conditions change.
Demolition controls vary with structure, condition, neighbours, retained elements and the chosen method.
A building record does not prove structural stability, service isolation, hazardous-material clearance or compliance with the written plan.
Scaffolds should be designed, erected, altered and dismantled only by competent people under competent supervision.
A scaffold should follow a recognised standard configuration or be supported by suitable design calculations.
Scaffolds require stable foundations, adequate bracing, safe access and suitable edge protection.
Platforms must be suitable for their intended loads and kept free from unsafe gaps or excessive stored materials.
Scaffolds must be inspected before first use and after events that could affect safety.
Construction scaffolds where a person could fall 2 metres or more require inspection at intervals not exceeding 7 days.
Unauthorised access to scaffolds and ladders should be prevented, especially when the site is unattended.
Alterations should only be made by authorised competent people and should preserve the scaffold's stability.
The presence of scaffolding does not establish that its design, ties, loading, access or inspection regime is compliant.
Inspection frequency and design requirements depend on scaffold type, use, height, loading, weather and configuration.
